summary: Specifies an optional Quick-Start mechanism where a transport protocol and routers cooperate to determine an allowed initial sending rate, and at times a rate after an idle period. It is designed for several transports but focuses on TCP. This RFC is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: Quick-Start lets a transport sender ask routers whether it may begin at a higher sending rate. The request succeeds only when the endpoints and routers along the path support and approve it.

questions: how to speed up tcp slow start
subtitle: An optional method for endpoints and routers to agree on a higher initial sending rate.

tldr.problem: TCP normally probes a path to learn how much data it can send, which can take time when the path has available capacity.
tldr.mechanism: A sender can put a requested rate in a Quick-Start IP option. Routers along the path approve, reduce, or deny the request, and the receiver returns the result to the sender in transport-level feedback.
tldr.outcome: The RFC proposes Quick-Start for controlled environments, not ubiquitous use across the global Internet. It is an Experimental protocol.

today: RFC 4782 is an Experimental RFC published in January 2007. Its metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the RFC presents Quick-Start as a mechanism for controlled environments rather than ubiquitous Internet deployment.

sections.title: Why Request a Sending Rate
sections.content:
TCP normally starts with an initial congestion window and increases it while probing for available capacity. The RFC notes that this process can take several round trips, which can matter for transfers that finish before the path is fully used.

Quick-Start lets a sender request a higher rate and asks routers along the path to approve it. The requested rate is not reserved capacity or preferential treatment; a router indicates that its output link appears underutilized.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP gradually tests how much data the path can carry. Quick-Start asks routers whether the sender can begin at a higher rate instead of waiting for the usual probing process.

sections.title: Request and Approval
sections.content:
The sender puts a requested rate and a Quick-Start Time to Live value in an IP option. Each router that supports and approves the request changes that value as specified. The receiver compares the returned value with the IP TTL and reports information to the sender.

If the sender confirms approval from the path, it converts the allowed rate and measured round-trip time into a congestion window and sends that data at a controlled pace. Otherwise it uses the transport's normal congestion-control behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers along the path indicate whether they approve the request. The receiver reports the result, and the sender uses a higher initial window only when the approval checks succeed.

sections.title: IP Options and the Nonce
sections.content:
The Quick-Start IP option carries the requested rate, a Quick-Start TTL, and a nonce. Routers can approve the requested rate, reduce it, or leave the request unapproved. If a router reduces the rate, it also changes the nonce.

For TCP, the receiver returns Quick-Start information in a TCP option. The sender uses the returned rate, TTL information, and nonce to check the response against its request.
sections.plainLanguage: The IP option carries the requested rate and a value used to check the response. TCP feedback tells the sender what rate the path approved, if any.

sections.title: Using Quick-Start with TCP
sections.content:
The RFC describes using Quick-Start during connection setup and, in some circumstances, during a connection after an idle period. The endpoints use the request and response options to determine whether the requested rate was approved.

Once the sender has sent the approved initial window, ordinary TCP congestion control governs later transmissions. If a Quick-Start request is not approved, the sender uses the normal TCP procedure.
sections.plainLanguage: Quick-Start can affect the initial sending rate, but it does not replace TCP congestion control. Normal control resumes after the approved initial data is sent.

sections.title: Limitations and Deployment
sections.content:
Quick-Start depends on support throughout the path. Routers or middleboxes that do not understand IP options may discard a request, and tunnels or changing paths can affect the checks used to determine approval.

The RFC discusses these limitations and concludes that Quick-Start may be useful in controlled environments. It does not propose the mechanism for ubiquitous deployment in the global Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: Every relevant part of a path must handle the request consistently. The RFC therefore presents Quick-Start as an option for controlled networks, not as a feature that can be assumed to work everywhere.

references.text: Allman, M., Floyd, S., and W. Stevens, "TCP Congestion Control", RFC 2581, April 1999.
